entry.summary: A prompt to a coding agent is a specification, even when it sounds like a conversation. The quality of the result depends on how much of the specification you state and how much the agent has to guess. Most bad output comes from guesses the author did not know they had left open. 1. One goal. "Add a product list page" is a goal. "Improve the shop" is a wish. Split large wishes into goals the agent can finish and check. 2. The files it may change. "Edit only src/pages/Products.tsx and its test" stops the agent from rewriting the app. Naming files also makes review faster. 3. What to leave alone. "Do not change the API shape or the routing" prevents quiet breakage. Agents are good at tidying things you did not ask them to touch. 4. A check it can run. entry.title: Everything You Need to Know About MCP
entry.summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI agents to the tools and data they need. Before MCP, every agent had its own way to call a database, read a file, or run a command, so each integration was built from scratch. MCP defines one protocol, so a server written once can serve any agent that speaks it. An MCP server offers three kinds of things: Tools are functions the agent can call, such as "run tests" or "query orders". Each tool has a name, a description, and a schema for its arguments. Resources are data the agent can read, such as a file, a document, or a log snapshot. Prompts are reusable templates the user or client can invoke. Most servers today mainly offer tools. The agent decides when to call them, based on their descriptions. A client, such as an I…
